quote: In 2016, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6--2 in *Gobeille v. Liberty Mutual Insurance Co.* that ERISA preempts state laws requiring self-insured employer health plans to report claims data into state all-payer databases.
correct_fact: Decided March 1, 2016; Kennedy for the Court joined by Roberts, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, Kagan; Ginsburg dissenting joined by Sotomayor (6-2). Holding: 'ERISA pre-empts Vermont's statute as applied to ERISA plans.'
source_quote: 'ERISA pre-empts Vermont's statute as applied to ERISA plans.' 'Kennedy, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. ... Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Sotomayor, J., joined.'

quote: That legal limitation became a concrete failure on January 1, 2023, when Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont---the state's largest private insurer---exercised its legal right to opt out and refused to renew its OneCare contract.
correct_fact: Gobeille concerns ERISA preemption of state data-reporting mandates for self-insured employer plans. BCBSVT's 2023 exit was a voluntary decision not to contract with OneCare for 2023 (talks over claims-data safeguards broke down); Vermont law never required insurers to contract with the ACO. Gobeille did not give BCBSVT a 'legal right to opt out', and it does not prevent the state from regulating fully insured carriers. The defensible link is narrower: ERISA puts self-insured employer plans largely beyond state compulsion, so the all-payer model rested on voluntary payer contracts.
source_quote: Gobeille: 'ERISA pre-empts Vermont's statute as applied to ERISA plans.' VTDigger: Blue Cross 'will not contract with OneCare Vermont in 2023'.
proposed_new_text: Because payer participation rested on voluntary contracts, that limit became a concrete failure on January 1, 2023, when Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont---the state's largest private insurer---declined to renew its OneCare contract.
notes: Same causal over-reach in Figure 1.1 Policy row ('Gobeille ... blocked state authority to compel self-insured commercial payers into the model' is fine for self-insured plans, but BCBSVT's fully insured book was not blocked by Gobeille) and in §1.10 'no management decision could reverse a federal court ruling'. Author decision; flagged, not a factual 'WRONG' because the sentence is framed as interpretation.

quote: OneCare Vermont ran for twelve years on a voluntary model: all 14 hospitals took part, but the insurers did not have to
correct_fact: OneCare's April 2023 overview to House Appropriations lists '14 hospitals' in its network for 2023 (~297,000 attributed). Caveats: (1) hospital participation varied by payer program -- Oliver Wyman (2024) wrote that 'OneCare participation is voluntary and doesn't include several hospitals and many community-based providers'; (2) OneCare's own deck says 'Formed in 2012', while VTDigger says it 'started as a for-profit entity in 2013' -- the 'twelve years / founded 2013' framing rests on VTDigger.
source_quote: '5,128 providers- 100% retention for 2023 • 14 hospitals | 82% of primary care' ; 'Formed in 2012 by the University of Vermont Medical Center and Dartmouth Hitchcock Health'. OW p.37: 'OneCare participation is voluntary and doesn't include several hospitals and many community-based providers'
notes: Figure 1.1 'Provider buy-in was achieved (all 14 hospitals)' rests on the same source. Founding year 2012 vs 2013 is a source conflict; lines 839/1306 ('2013--2025') could say 'founded in 2012-13' or simply drop the year count.

quote: Internal Recognition: OneCare's own leadership acknowledged to Green Mountain Care Board regulators that its analytics infrastructure lagged behind newer systems being adopted by member health networks.
correct_fact: At its November 2022 budget presentation, OneCare staff told GMCB its current data analytics system was not as effective as software UVM Health Network was starting to use, and that subcontracting would be cheaper. (Staff, not specifically 'leadership'; one network -- UVMHN -- not 'member health networks' generally.)
source_quote: OneCare staff told state regulators at a November budget presentation that 'its current data analytics system is not as effective as software that UVM Health Network is starting to use'
proposed_new_text: Internal Recognition: OneCare staff told Green Mountain Care Board regulators in November 2022 that its analytics system was not as effective as the software UVM Health Network was starting to use.
notes: Optional precision edit.

quote: Its all-payer model put essentially every hospital in the state --- 52 of them --- under global budgets beginning in 2014, mandatorily, with no opt-out.
correct_fact: RTI's final evaluation: by July 2014 all 46 general acute care hospitals were under global budgets (covering 95% of hospital revenue); a 47th (Holy Cross Germantown) opened Oct 2014 and got a budget from July 2015.
source_quote: 'By July 2014, all 46 general acute care hospitals in the state were operating under a global budget, with global budgets encompassing 95 percent of hospital revenue.'
proposed_new_text: Its all-payer model put every general acute care hospital in the state --- 46 of them --- under global budgets by July 2014, with no opt-out.

quote: Medicare spending fell 2.8% against a comparison group, driven by a 4.1% reduction in hospital expenditures --- more than \$780 million saved. Potentially preventable admissions fell 16.1%, unplanned readmissions 9.5%.
correct_fact: RTI (Nov 2019, first 4.5 years): Medicare total expenditures grew 2.8% more slowly than the comparison group ($975M savings), largely from 4.1% slower growth in hospital expenditures ($796M). Admissions for ambulatory-care-sensitive conditions fell 6.7% more than the comparison group (Medicare); the difference in unplanned readmissions was NOT statistically significant. The 16.1% and 9.5% figures do not appear in the RTI evaluation.
source_quote: 'Medicare beneficiaries had 2.8 percent slower growth in total expenditures ($975 million in savings) ... largely driven by 4.1 percent slower growth in total hospital expenditures ($796 million in savings)'; 'Although the rate of hospital admissions for ACSCs fell by 6.7 percent more in Maryland than in the comparison group, the difference in the reduction in unplanned readmissions was not statistically significant.'
proposed_new_text: Medicare spending grew 2.8% more slowly than in a comparison group --- about \$975 million saved over the first four and a half years --- driven by 4.1% slower growth in hospital expenditures. Admissions for ambulatory-care-sensitive conditions fell 6.7% more than in the comparison group, though the drop in unplanned readmissions was no larger than elsewhere.
notes: Next sentence ('readmissions improved for healthier patients while hospitals struggled with sicker ones') is consistent with RTI's finding that teaching/high-DSH hospitals had poorer readmission outcomes. 'Population health measures did not move' is from Milbank's summary; not verified in RTI text here -- leave or soften.

quote: Maryland HSCRC early period: global budgets without adequate primary care produced pressure without sustainable improvement.
correct_fact: RTI's evaluation of 2014-2018 found savings and an ACSC admission decline (i.e., some improvement), and no source located characterizes the early period as 'pressure without sustainable improvement'; it also sits uneasily with the chapter's own BEYOND VERMONT box citing Maryland savings. Maryland's later TCOC model (2019) added the Maryland Primary Care Program, which supports the 'primary care was missing' reading only loosely.
source_quote: 'Admissions for ambulatory care sensitive conditions (ACSCs) decreased 6.7 percent more for Medicare beneficiaries in Maryland than in the comparison group'
proposed_new_text: Maryland's 2014--2018 all-payer model: hospital spending fell against comparison groups, but without a primary care program until 2019, population-level gains were modest.
notes: Searched RTI final evaluation text; no support for the original wording.

quote: The Blueprint's 5.8:1 return on investment --- \$5.8 million in reduced medical expenditure per \$1 million invested in primary care --- is achievable because
correct_fact: 5.8:1 is a dated estimate: Jones et al. (Milbank Quarterly, 2016) -- 'Based on an annualized cost-gain ratio, medical expenditures decreased by approximately $5.8 million for every $1 million spent on the Blueprint initiative' -- and DVHA's estimated all-payer ROI for CY2014 (5.8, budget-based; Medicaid-only 0.9 with SMS / 3.0 without). The Blueprint's later all-payer estimate, for 2016, is $3 saved per $1 including Special Medicaid Services and $3.8 excluding them (Blueprint ROI summary to Senate Health & Welfare, Jan 20, 2023). The investment is the Blueprint initiative (PCMH + CHT payments + program budget), not 'primary care' generally.
source_quote: 'The estimated return on investment for all payers for 2016 is • $3 saved for every dollar spent including SMS (Special Medicaid services) • $3.8 saved for every dollar spent excluding SMS' ; 'Based on an annualized cost-gain ratio, medical expenditures decreased by approximately $5.8 million for every $1 million spent on the Blueprint initiative.' ; DVHA 2016: 'Estimated Return on Investment for All Payers in Calendar Year 2014 ... Return on investment 5.8'
proposed_new_text: The Blueprint's estimated returns --- about \$5.8 in reduced medical expenditure per \$1 spent on the initiative in 2014, and \$3 to \$3.8 per \$1 in the Blueprint's 2016 estimate --- are achievable because
notes: 5.8:1 recurs at lines 1195, 1310, 1434, 1457, 1533 and is repeated across the book; decide once whether to keep 5.8 with its date or switch to the later 3-3.8 range.

quote: Vermont's Blueprint for Health generated a 5.8-to-1 return on investment from its primary care investment --- among the most robust ROI findings in the value-based care literature.
correct_fact: 5.8:1 is a 2014 estimate (later 2016 estimate $3-$3.8 per $1). No source found ranking it 'among the most robust ROI findings in the value-based care literature'; DVHA notes the CY2014 figure uses budgeted rather than actual program spending.
source_quote: DVHA 2016: 'Also note the budgeted amount does not reflect actual programmatic expenditures'
proposed_new_text: Vermont's Blueprint for Health estimated a return of roughly \$5.8 for every \$1 spent on the initiative in 2014, and \$3 to \$3.8 per \$1 in its 2016 estimate.
notes: Superlative fails the 'source or delete' rule.

quote: Act 51 moved from diagnosis to planning, authorizing AHS to run transformation engagements with individual hospitals.
correct_fact: Act 51 of 2023 (H.206), Sec. 8 added Act 167 Sec. 2a: AHS 'shall engage in transformation planning with up to four hospitals'. Note Act 51 is mostly a DVHA miscellany (adult dental, liens, etc.); the hospital-planning piece is one section.
source_quote: 'Sec. 8. 2022 Acts and Resolves No. 167, Sec. 2a is added to read: ... (a) The Agency of Human Services shall engage in transformation planning with up to four hospitals, or other number of hospitals if possible with alternate funds'
notes: Optional precision: 'with up to four hospitals'.

quote: Act 55 drug cap (\$135M savings)
correct_fact: Act 55 of 2025 (H.266) caps hospital charges to insurers for outpatient/office-administered drugs at 120% of ASP, effective January 1, 2026 (also requires 340B reporting). No primary source found for '$135M savings'; Chapter 6 (line 3223) of this book gives a different figure ($104.3M from the Act 55 drug cap in FY2026). Internal inconsistency.
source_quote: § 9407(a)(1): 'A hospital shall not submit a claim to a health insurer for reimbursement of a prescription drug administered in an outpatient or office setting in an amount that exceeds 120 percent of the average sales price (ASP)'; Sec. 6: '... shall take effect on January 1, 2026.'
proposed_new_text: Act 55 outpatient drug-price cap (120% of ASP, from January 2026)
notes: Searched GMCB HROC slides (Dec 4 2025) and legislature: no $135M. Chapter 2 line 2044 says 'effective April 2025' -- wrong (April 1, 2025 is the ASP reference date; cap effective Jan 1, 2026).

quote: Act 55 (drug pricing); Act 49 (insurer solvency); Act 62 (HIE governance)
correct_fact: Act 55 of 2025 (H.266): 340B reporting + 120% ASP outpatient drug charge cap. Act 49 of 2025 (H.482): GMCB authority to reduce a hospital's reimbursement rates when a domestic insurer's solvency is threatened, and to appoint a hospital observer. Act 62 of 2025 (S.63): modifies GMCB regulatory duties, including moving the statewide HIT Plan to DVHA with its HIE Steering Committee.
source_quote: Act 49: 'An act relating to Green Mountain Care Board authority to adjust a hospital's reimbursement rates and to appoint a hospital observer' (§ 9384 'RISKS TO HEALTH INSURER SOLVENCY'). Act 62: 'The Department of Vermont Health Access, in consultation with the Department's Health Information Exchange Steering Committee, shall be responsible for the overall coordination of Vermont's statewide Health Information Technology Plan.'
notes: Figure 1.5 caption says 'Acts 167, 51, 55, 62, 68 of 2022--2025' -- omits Act 49 which the table cites; add it.

quote: Roughly two dozen states operate an established all-payer claims database (APCD Council); the other half of the country does not have one.
correct_fact: Per the APCD Council (as cited by Colorado HCPF, Aug 27, 2026), 24 states have an APCD.
source_quote: 'According to the APCD Council, 24 states have an APCD.'
notes: Secondary citation of the APCD Council; the Council's own map page (apcdcouncil.org/state/map) shows no counts in text form.

quote: Essex County's elevated uninsurance rate and limited primary care access are equity problems with a clinical solution
correct_fact: Essex had the highest county uninsured rate in the 2014 Vermont Household Health Insurance Survey (10% vs 3.7% statewide). Data are old; no newer VDH county figure found.
source_quote: (via search summary) 'The highest uninsured rates occur in Essex (10%) and Caledonia (6.6%) counties.'
notes: Quote obtained via search summary, not a full read of the PDF; low-stakes, but re-verify against ACS SAHIE before print. Same box: 'certifying additional CCBHCs in Northeast Kingdom communities' -- NKHS was certified July 1, 2026, so it is done, not prospective.

quote: Vermont's race/ethnicity data in VHCURES is incomplete --- commercial claims frequently lack demographic fields.
correct_fact: GMCB (2021): 'Each payer may or may not collect race and ethnicity data. Submission of race and ethnicity to GMCB is currently optional.' (2021 is the latest primary statement found; status may have changed.)
source_quote: 'VHCURES Each payer may or may not collect race and ethnicity data. Submission of race and ethnicity to GMCB is currently optional.'
notes: Applies to all payers, not only commercial.

quote: The Vermont Department of Health's Health Equity Data Report (January 2025) documents this limitation explicitly.
correct_fact: VDH's Health Equity Data 2025 report (Jan 15, 2025) does not mention VHCURES or missing race fields in claims. It says only that the Department's data sources (surveys, registries, insurance claims, discharge data) are 'not all integrated and standardized', limiting equity analysis. The explicit VHCURES statement is GMCB's (Feb 2021 testimony on H.210).
source_quote: VDH 2025: 'The data owned and used by the Department is not all integrated and standardized. This limitation impacts the Department's ability to take its existing data and complete a comprehensive analysis that measures health equity across lines of race, ethnicity, ...'
proposed_new_text: The Green Mountain Care Board has told the legislature that submitting race and ethnicity data to VHCURES is optional for payers, and the Vermont Department of Health's Health Equity Data report (January 2025) notes that the state's health data sources are not integrated or standardized enough for comprehensive equity analysis.

quote: The Vermont CIN's shared services model addresses this: a shared analytics and IT function within the CIN provides all 14 hospitals access to Technology pillar capability they cannot individually afford.
correct_fact: In Vermont's RHT application, 'Establishing a Clinically Integrated Network of Shared Services' is one of five initiative categories -- a set of grant activities (incentives for a VOLUNTARY shared EMR building on the VHIE, statewide e-Consult, RPM grants, telehealth grants, AI-scribe grants, team-based care capacity, shared HR systems). No source describes a CIN entity with 'a shared analytics and IT function' that 'provides all 14 hospitals access'; analytics support for transformation planning is a separate state vendor procurement. Present tense overstates: these are funded intentions, subject to change.
source_quote: 'The state's key initiatives include: (1) Regionalization and Innovative Care Strategies ("Regionalization"); (2) Establishing a Clinically Integrated Network of Shared Services ("Shared Services"); ...' ; '9 Incentivizing adoption of a shared EMR platform ... Build upon Vermont's existing health data infrastructure, including Vermont's Health Information Exchange (VHIE)'; 'items listed in the tables below are subject to change'
proposed_new_text: The shared-services track of Vermont's RHT Program is aimed at exactly this: incentives for a voluntary shared EMR built on the state's health information exchange, plus grants for e-Consult, remote monitoring, telehealth and AI scribes, so smaller hospitals and practices can reach Technology pillar capability they cannot individually afford.
notes: Same overstatement in line 1420 ('The Vermont CIN provides shared capability to rural hospitals') -- make prospective ('is meant to provide'). Lines 1338 and 1551 ('Vermont CIN (RHT Program)', 'Vermont CIN under development') are acceptable. Also: Gifford, Grace Cottage and North Country are CAHs (confirmed by AHS table), but no source checked for 'limited IT staff'.

quote: deploying telehealth through the RHT Program to reduce geographic access barriers
correct_fact: RHT activity 12: grants to rural independent medical practices to adopt telehealth technology (not broadband).
source_quote: '12 Grant funds to providers to adopt telehealth technology. Provide grants to rural independent medical practices to purchase and implement telehealth technology solutions statewide ... (Note: funds will not be used for broadband).'
